newsitem.title: INDIA: Blanket security in Kashmir ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Blanket security in Kashmir ahead of polls.

text.p: Some 200,000 Indian security officers fanned out across Kashmir on Friday ahead of the first local elections since a separatist rebellion erupted six years ago.
Voting in the first stage of elections to the Jammu and Kashmir state assembly was set for Saturday in 26 of the 87 constituencies in the Himalayan state.
The rest of the state will vote on three days later this month -- September 16, 21 and 30 -- to allow polling officers and armed security forces to move between regions.
Polling is taking place four months after an Indian general election, in which the northern state chose six representatives to sit in the lower house of parliament in New Delhi.
This month's balloting is designed to produce the first state assembly since the separatist insurgency erupted in 1990.
It is viewed as a crucial test of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's strategy for restoring democratic rule to the region.

Militant groups in mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state have been fighting either for independence or merger with neighbouring Pakistan, which rules one third of the Kashmir region and stakes a claim over the rest.
The last state assembly, elected in 1987 amid widespread allegations of rigging, was dissolved in early 1990 to allow New Delhi to impose direct rule.
India deployed tens of thousands of army and paramilitary troops to try to quell the revolt.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence.
Former state chief minister Farooq Abdullah, head of the largest pro-India party, the National Conference, says some 50,000 people have died.
Indian officials say an unrelenting crackdown by security forces has taken its toll on militants.
"New recruitment of militants has almost dried out," General J.S. Dhillon, head of army forces in the region, told reporters earlier this week.
He said militant groups were becoming increasingly dependent on foreign mercenaries.
The All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, comprising some 30 leading separatist groups, accused government-backed militants of threatening to punish voters if they did not vote.
During the parliamentary elections in May, human rights groups alleged widespread coercion. Government officials denied the charges.
Hurriyat leaders have toured the Kashmir Valley, a focus of the rebellion, urging voters to boycott the assembly polls.
Hurriyat chiefs said they had been detained by security four times in the past two weeks, and beaten.
Most businesses and shops were closed on Friday in Srinagar, the state's summer capital, following a call by the Hurriyat for a two-day protest strike.
Authorities charged the Hurriyat with intimidating voters.
"They are going around asking people not to vote," state chief secretary Ashok Kumar said. "We have to do something about it."
Kumar would not say whether the Hurriyat leaders would be detained or placed under house arrest on Saturday to prevent them from leading public protests.

The National Conference charged government-backed militants supporting rival candidates with killing nine of their activists in the past week. It asked the federal Election Commission to send special observers to sensitive polling stations.
But authorities shrugged off the allegations. "Some renegade militants say they are being harassed," Kumar said, referring to former militants now supporting the government.
"It is not such a simple black and white story," he added.
